relationship: Thematic parallel: imperial conquest and pride
rationale: Alexander's plundering of many nations and lifted-up heart are comparable to the Assyrian ruler's lofty pride and boast of seizing the inhabited world and plundering nations. The connection is the conjunction of expansive conquest, spoil and self-exaltation; Isaiah's ruler, explicitly identified as Assyrian, is not identified with Alexander.

relationship: Literary parallel: communal mourning across generations
rationale: Maccabees depicts elders groaning and young women weakened in Israel's mourning; Lamentations depicts Zion's elders in dust and sackcloth and Jerusalem's leading virgins brought to the ground. Both give communal calamity a visible expression among elders and young women, without describing the same catastrophe.

relationship: Thematic parallel: altered beauty in calamity
rationale: Maccabees includes the changed beauty of women in the account of national mourning. Isaiah portrays fragrance, head adornment and decorated clothing giving way to dust, baldness and sackcloth. The comparison concerns the loss of an adorned appearance in calamity; Maccabees does not specify Isaiah's individual changes.

relationship: Literary parallel: bridal life interrupted by communal distress
rationale: Maccabees brings the bridegroom and the bride in her bridal chamber into Israel's lament. Joel calls the bridegroom from his bedroom and the bride from her bridal chamber into the gathered community, where priests weep for the people. Both extend communal distress into bridal life, though Joel commands an assembly and Maccabees reports mourning.

relationship: Thematic parallel: incense to foreign gods throughout urban life
rationale: The incense at house doors and in squares follows the establishment of pagan altars in Maccabees. Jeremiah similarly depicts Judah's cities burning incense to foreign gods and Jerusalem's many exits associated with incense altars to Baal. Both present foreign worship spread through inhabited places; the doors and squares are not equated with Jeremiah's exits or assigned his named deity.

relationship: Narrative parallel: sacred writings cut apart and burned
rationale: The persecutors tear the books of the law and burn them; Jehoiakim cuts columns from the roll of Jeremiah's words and burns the whole roll. Both express hostility to divine instruction by physically dividing and burning its written document. The law books and Jeremiah's prophetic roll are different writings in different incidents.

relationship: Wisdom parallel: praised remembrance of righteous deeds
rationale: The praise of Judas joins deeds that gladden Jacob to a memory that remains a blessing. Proverbs describes the memory of righteous people as accompanied by praises, in contrast to the extinguished name of the impious. The proverb illuminates the favorable remembrance expressed in the tribute to Judas.

relationship: Thematic parallel: accepting God's will amid readiness to face death
rationale: Judas concludes his willingness to face death in battle by affirming that Heaven's will will be done. After Paul declares his readiness to die for the Lord Jesus, his companions yield with the words that the Lord's will be done. The shared movement is from readiness for mortal danger to acceptance of divine will; the speakers and conflicts differ.

relationship: Thematic parallel: human plans subject to divine will
rationale: Judas prepares for the coming battle but leaves its outcome to the will in heaven. James corrects confident plans for tomorrow by saying that both continued life and action depend on the Lord's will. Both qualify human intention by divine will, without equating Judas's battle preparation with the trading plans James addresses.

relationship: Narrative parallel: smoke reveals a military reversal
rationale: The detachment looking from the mountain recognizes its side's defeat from the visible smoke of the burning camp. At Ai, inhabitants and Joshua's force see the city's rising smoke, and Israel turns against Ai's men. In both battles smoke makes the capture and burning of a position visible to forces outside it; the tactics and the subsequent ability to flee differ.

relationship: Thematic parallel: priestly integrity and devotion to the law
rationale: Judas chooses blameless priests devoted to the law for the cleansing of the holy places. Malachi's account of faithful priestly service joins truthful law and freedom from injustice to the priest's duty to guard knowledge and provide law. This connects the qualities sought in the chosen priests with the described priestly vocation, not with a second account of their appointment.

relationship: Thematic parallel: a coordinated plan to destroy Jews in one day
rationale: The report from Gilead describes an arranged assault intended to destroy the confined people in a single day. Esther's letters likewise schedule the destruction of the Jews on one day. The connection is the concentrated timetable for destroying a Jewish population, while the local siege plan and empire-wide decree remain distinct.

relationship: Narrative contrast: treatment of those lagging on a journey
rationale: Judas gathers those who lag behind and encourages the company on the road to Judah. Deuteronomy recalls Amalek attacking the weary people at Israel's rear on the journey from Egypt. The concrete contrast is care for stragglers against exploitation of the rear's vulnerability; Judas is not presented as consciously reenacting that earlier journey.

relationship: Imagery parallel: an army flashing like fiery torches
rationale: Maccabees likens sunlight reflected from the army's golden and bronze shields to torches of fire shining on the mountains. Nahum likens the appearance of chariots in the roads and squares to fiery torches and flashing lightning. The shared comparison conveys the dazzling appearance of military equipment, while the equipment, setting and movement differ.
